Ireland Marks Six Years Since 2018 Cyber Attack on National Payments System

DUBLIN—This week marks six years since the unprecedented cyber attack that disrupted Ireland’s national payments infrastructure in 2018, halting transactions across the retail and services sectors and highlighting the country’s vulnerability to digital threats.

On 13 June 2018, a sophisticated malware campaign targeted the RealPay Network, which processes the bulk of debit and credit card transactions nationwide. The attack forced the shutdown of payment terminals at thousands of shops, restaurants, and public transport providers, leaving consumers unable to pay with cards for several hours. The Central Bank later estimated that daily retail sales fell by 45% on the day of the attack, while ATM withdrawals surged by 38% as consumers scrambled for cash.

The government quickly convened its National Cyber Security Taskforce and, working with RealPay and partners across Europe, restored core payment services within 12 hours. However, the incident prompted calls for urgent investment in digital resilience. “It was a wake-up call for the entire economy,” said Fiona Doran, then president of the Irish Retail Association. “The shockwaves were felt on every high street.”

The source of the attack was never publicly confirmed, though cybersecurity analysts at InfoGuard Ireland linked it to a criminal syndicate operating in Eastern Europe. No data breaches or customer losses were reported, but RealPay’s CEO at the time, Alan Keane, conceded that “far more robust defences” were needed to protect critical infrastructure.

In the aftermath, the government allocated €45 million to bolster cybersecurity in 2019 and introduced mandatory incident reporting for payment providers. “Ireland is now better prepared, but the risks remain,” said Dr. Seamus Kerr, a cybersecurity lecturer at University College Dublin. “The 2018 attack was disruptive but ultimately contained. The next one could be worse if we let our guard down.” 

No disruptions to payment systems have been reported since.
